title: कठोपनिषत् — Kaṭha Upaniṣad
subtitle: Naciketas at the House of Death
summary: An Upaniṣad of the Kaṭha school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, in two adhyāyas of three vallīs: a boy given to Death waits at his door, refuses every reward, and is taught what remains of a person when the body falls — the self that is not born and does not die.
opening: What remains of a person after death? Why is the good not the same as the pleasant? What is it that is ‘not born and does not die’? Who is fit to be taught it, and why can it not be learnt by cleverness or much hearing alone?
facts: Two adhyāyas of three vallīs each: 29, 25 and 17 mantras in the first; 15, 15 and 18 in the second — 119 mantras in all

The mūla of Śaṅkara’s commentary (Advaita Sharada) as base, collated with GRETIL’s text (after Olivelle 1998), the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text; three slips of the base corrected, every difference classified

The first adhyāya — its three vallīs: Naciketas and the three boons; the good and the pleasant; the chariot — is analysed: every mantra with the Sanskrit, padaccheda, word-by-word grammar, translations and the commentaries, with nine studies. The second adhyāya shows the verified text, with the analysis in preparation
objectives: Read the first adhyāya in Sanskrit with a transliteration you can trust, and know what each word is doing.
Tell the story of Naciketas — the sacrifice, the gift to Death, the three nights and the three boons — and say what each boon asks for.
Explain how Śaṅkara, Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva’s school read the third question differently: a self beyond the body, the released self, or the Lord in the released.
Say why the commentators read Death’s offers as a test, and what the boy’s refusal shows about who is fit to be taught.
Say what separates the good from the pleasant, why the teaching is said to need a teacher and not reasoning alone, and how the commentators read ‘whom he chooses’.

Explain the image of the chariot and the ladder from the senses to the person, and say how Śaṅkara, Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva read the two in the cave and the ‘unmanifest’ — and why none of them takes it as Sāṅkhya’s primal matter.
Tell the ancient text from the modern voice explaining it, on any page.

key_questions.q: Why does a story about a sacrifice open a teaching about the self?
What does the boy offer, and why does his father give him to Death?
What are the three boons, and why three?
What is the third question really asking?
Why does Death try to change the boy’s mind?
What does the boy’s refusal show?
What is the difference between the good and the pleasant?
Why is Om the answer to a question about what lies beyond dharma and adharma?
What is it that is ‘not born and does not die’, and who chooses whom?
Who are the two who ‘drink the truth’ in the cave?
What does the image of the chariot teach?
What lies beyond the senses, and why is there nothing beyond the person?
Why is the path called a razor’s edge?

reading_guide.title: Adhyāya 1, vallī 1: Naciketas and the three boons (analysed).
reading_guide.text: The sacrifice, the gift to Death, three nights at Death’s door, the three boons, and the refusal of every reward.

reading_guide.title: Adhyāya 1, vallī 2: the good and the pleasant (analysed).
reading_guide.text: Death begins to teach: the two paths, the teacher and the limits of reasoning, Om, the self that is not born and does not die, and how it is — and is not — obtained.

reading_guide.title: Adhyāya 1, vallī 3: the chariot (analysed).
reading_guide.text: The self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the senses as horses; the ladder from the senses to the person beyond which there is nothing; ‘arise, awake’.

reading_guide.title: Adhyāya 2, vallī 1: turning inward.
reading_guide.text: The senses face outward; the wise turn their gaze within; what is here is there.

reading_guide.title: Adhyāya 2, vallī 2: the city of eleven gates.
reading_guide.text: The self in the body, the one in the many, and the light by which all else shines.

reading_guide.title: Adhyāya 2, vallī 3: the eternal tree.
reading_guide.text: The aśvattha with its roots above, the discipline of yoga, and Naciketas’ attaining of Brahman.

sections.heading: The name and its place
sections.label: linguistic
paras: The Upaniṣad belongs to the Kaṭha school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; its parts are called vallīs, ‘creepers’, as in the Taittirīya. Śaṅkara begins his commentary by calling it ‘the vallīs of the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad’ and promising a short explanation: «अथ काठकोपनिषद्वल्लीनां सुखार्थप्रबोधनार्थमल्पग्रन्था वृत्तिरारभ्यते».

He also explains the word upaniṣad itself, from the root sad with upa and ni: «सदेर्धातोर्विशरणगत्यवसादनार्थस्योपनिपूर्वस्य क्विप्प्रत्ययान्तस्य रूपमिदम्» — the knowledge that loosens, leads and destroys the seed of rebirth.

sections.heading: Why the Kaṭha matters
sections.label: traditional
paras: Śaṅkara’s first words salute the two figures of the dialogue as teacher and pupil of the knowledge of Brahman: «ॐ नमो भगवते वैवस्वताय मृत्यवे ब्रह्मविद्याचार्याय, नचिकेतसे च» — ‘to Death, son of Vivasvat, teacher of the knowledge of Brahman, and to Naciketas’.

He names the goal from the Upaniṣad’s own words: one who has perceived the self is freed from the mouth of Death — «निचाय्य तं मृत्युमुखात्प्रमुच्यते» — and Naciketas, at the end, attains Brahman — «ब्रह्म प्राप्तो विरजोऽभूद्विमृत्युः». Raṅgarāmānuja opens his Prakāśikā with the modest promise to explain ‘the Kaṭha vallīs as best he can’: «व्याख्यास्ये विदुषां प्रीत्यै कठवल्लीं यथामति».

sections.heading: A narrative introduction
sections.label: direct
paras: A father gives away all he owns at a sacrifice, but the cows are worn out. His son asks to whom he himself will be given, and the father, angry, answers: to Death. The boy waits three nights at Death’s house without food; Death offers three boons. The boy asks for his father’s good will, for the fire that leads to heaven, and for knowledge of what remains of a man after death. Death tries to withdraw the last, offering every pleasure instead; the boy refuses them all.

Then Death teaches. The good and the pleasant are different, and the wise choose the good: «श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतः». The self is not born and does not die. It is the rider of a chariot whose horses are the senses: «आत्मानं रथिनं विद्धि शरीरं रथमेव तु». The senses face outward, and the wise turn within. The world is a tree whose root is above: «ऊर्ध्वमूलोऽवाक्शाख एषोऽश्वत्थः सनातनः». The last mantra says that Naciketas, having received this knowledge from Death, attained Brahman: «मृत्युप्रोक्तां नचिकेतोऽथ लब्ध्वा».

sections.heading: The Kaṭha and the Gītā
sections.label: comparative

parallels.quote: अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते

paras: Two mantras of the second vallī recur almost word for word in the second chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā. The second half of 1.2.18, «अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे», is the second half of Gītā 2.20; and 1.2.19 ends, as Gītā 2.19 does, «उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते».
The first halves differ, and the shared wording does not by itself show which text drew on which. Both mantras are analysed with the second vallī; the sixth study sets the two texts side by side.

sections.heading: Three commentaries, three questions
sections.label: comparative
paras: The commentators read the same words as asking different things. At the third boon, Śaṅkara takes the doubt to be whether a self exists beyond body, senses and mind, and says the teaching that follows is the knowledge of the oneness of self and Brahman — «ब्रह्मात्मैकत्वविज्ञानं». Raṅgarāmānuja takes ‘one who has gone’ to be the released self: «सर्वबन्धविनिर्मोक्षाभिप्रायम्». Madhva glosses the question as about the Lord present in the released as their controller: «प्रेते मुक्ते मनुष्ये नियामकत्वेन भगवानस्तीति ज्ञानिनो वदन्ति».
This edition gives each reading in the commentator’s own words, says where they differ, and does not make any one of them the meaning of the text.

open_questions: The text printed with Raṅgarāmānuja has one more mantra in the first vallī than the base and the other witnesses; its manuscript basis needs a printed edition.
Madhva’s commentary is used from a digital text with frequent slips; it should be read against a printed edition.
Madhva’s bhāṣya, in the digital text used here, has no comment on 1.3.3–1.3.9 or 1.3.14–1.3.17, and gaps in its comment on 1.3.1–1.3.2.
